ABSTRACT
Background: Our previous studies found that Pure total flavnoids from citrus (PTFC) can effectively improve non-
alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) in mice. Here, we discuss on the mechanism of PTFC in treating NASH with
focus on the regulation of the gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism.
Methods: C57BL/6 J mice were randomly divided into three groups: normal diet group (Normal), high-fat diet
group (HFD) and high-fat + PTFC treatment group (PTFC). Mice in the Normal group were fed chow diet, while
the other groups were fed high fat diet (HFD) for 16 weeks. In the 5th week, the mice in the PTFC group were
treated with 50 mg/kg/day PTFC for an additional twelve weeks. After sacrifice, histopathology of the liver was
assessed, and the gut microbial composition was analyzed by 16S rDNA gene sequencing. Bile Acid profiles in
serum were determined by ultraperformance liquid chromatography (UPLC-MS/MS).
Results: PTFC intervention significantly attenuated HFD-induced NASH symptoms compared with the HFD group
in mice. 16S rDNA sequencing showed that PTFC treatment increased the phylogenetic diversity of the HFD-
induced microbiota dysbiosis. PTFC intervention significantly increased the relative abundances of Bacter -
oidaceae and Christensenellaceae. Furthermore, PTFC reduced the content of toxic bile acids, such as TDCA,
DCA, TCA, CA and increased the ratio of secondary to primary bile acids. FXR and TGR5 deficiency were
significantly alleviated.
Conclusion: PTFC can improve NASH via the the gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism.

1. Introduction
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common
chronic liver disease worldwide, affecting up to 25 % of adults and
children [ 1 – 3 ]. The spectrum of NAFLD ranges from simple nonalco -
holic fatty liver (NAFL) to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which
can progress to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma
(HCC) [ 4 , 5 ]. NASH is strongly associated with obesity and
obesity-related metabolic disorders [ 6 , 7 ].
Recently, many studies have demonstrated the pivotal role of the
“ gut-liver ” axis in NASH pathogenesis. The gut microbiota, the foun -
dational element of the gut-liver axis, plays vital roles in the regulation
of NASH by producing bacterial metabolites such as short-chain fatty
acids, secondary bile acids, and trimethylamine [ 8 , 9 ]. Bile acid (BA) is
typically associated with the gut microbiota and synthesized in the liver
from cholesterol and metabolized in the gut. Puri et al. [ 10 ] reported
that the srum BA profile in NASH patients was characterized by a
decreased ratio of secondary to primary BA. Farnesoid X receptor (FXR)
and the G protein-coupled bile acid receptor 5 (TGR5) are bile acid re -
ceptors that are important for bile acid and fat metabolism, as well as
in fl ammation, and have proven to be potential therapeutic targets for
NASH [ 11 ].
Pure total flavonoids from citrus (PTFC) were isolated and purified
from the dried and mature peel of Citrus Varieties (Changshan Huyou) in
Changshan and Quzhou of Zhejiang province, China. PTFC is composed
of naringin, neohesperidin and narirutin, the total content of flavonoids
is over 76 %. Naringin can reduce lipid synthesis, improve lipid depo -
sition and reduce inflammatory cell infiltration in the liver of rats
induced by high-fat diet [ 12 – 14 ]. The bioactive naringin is the main
metabolite of naringin in human intestinal microbial environment,
which indicates that the microbiota play an important role in regulating
the pharmacological action of naringin [ 15 ]. Our previous studies
showed that PTFC prevented the progression of NASH by regulating the
TLR/CCL and VEGF-C signaling pathway [ 16 , 17 ].
As far as we know, limited studies are focusing on the effects of PTFC
on the gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism. In the present study, we
examined whether PTFC could attenuate features of HFD-induced NASH
in mice, which might be related to the modulation of the gut microbiota
and bile acid metabolism.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Animals and treatments
A total of 18 wild type C57BL/6 J mice (6 – 8 weeks of age, male)
were purchased from Shanghai Sippr-BK Laboratory Animal Co. Ltd.
(production license: SCXK (Hu) 2013-0016). All experimental proced -
ures were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Zhejiang Chinese
Medical University and the National Guidelines for Experimental Ani -
mal Welfare.
Mice were housed in individually ventilated cages, provided with
water and standard/high-fat chow, and monitored daily for health and
clinical signs. All mice were randomly divided into three groups: normal
diet group (Normal), high-fat diet group (HFD), and high-fat
diet + PTFC treatment group (PTFC). In the 5th week, the PTFC group
was treated with 50 mg/kg/day PTFC for an additional twelve weeks. At
the endpoint of 16 weeks, the mice were anesthetized with sodium
pentobarbital (50 mg/kg). The mice were euthanized from exsangui -
nation, blood samples were extracted intraocularly, and fresh stool
samples were collected in sealed containers and immediately stored at
80
◦
C with prior snap-freezing in liquid nitrogen until DNA extraction.
2.2. Hematoxylin – eosin (HE) staining
Fresh liver specimens were processed according to a standard HE
staining technique [ 18 ]. Briefly, liver tissues were fixed by 10 % neutral
formalin, dehydrated in ethanol, and then embedded. Subsequently,
liver sections were stained with HE for pathological changes under an
optical microscope. Tissues were scored according to the criteria for
evaluating changes in fat and inflammation. Pathologists examined
sections to detect the presence of fat, necrosis, and inflammation.
2.3. Preparation of PTFC
Pure total flavonoids from citrus were prepared as previously
described [ 16 ]. In short, 1600 mL 0.1 % calcium carbonate solution was
used to extract every 100 g Changshan Huyou twice at 100 ℃ , extracting
for 1.5 h, filtering and steaming. The residue was dissolved in 10 times
volume of distilled water (30 mL), eluted with 2 times volume of resin
ethanol (elution concentration: 0%, 30 %, 50 %, 70 % and 90 %) at the
rate of 1 mL / min, and eluted with HPD-300 macroporous resin column
(volume: 100 mL, weight ratio: 1:20). The part with an elution con -
centration of 30 % was collected, concentrated and used after drying,
named PTFC. The main flavonoids were determined by High Perfor -
mance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) Analysis. The total flavonoid
content was calculated as 76.22 %.
2.4. Detection and analysis of gut microbiota in mice
DNA from faecal samples was extracted using a QIAamp ® DNA Stool
Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden,Germany). The resulting DNA was amplified
with specific barcoded bacterial primers targeting the V3-V4 hyper -
variable region of the 16S rDNA gene using primers: forward primer (5-
CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG-3) and reverse primer (5-GACTACHVGGG -
TATCTAATCC-3). The PCR reaction was carried out as follows: initial
denaturation at 94
◦
C for 2 min,followed by 25 cycles of denaturation at
94
◦
C for 30 s,annealing at 55
◦
C for 30 s, elongation at 72
◦
C for 1 min,
and finally, 72
◦
C for 10 min.
For each faecal sample, sequencing and bioinformatics were carried
out by Genesky Biotechnologies Inc. (Shanghai, China) on the Illumina
MiSeq platform to generate 2 × 250 bp paired-end reads. The remaining
unique reads were clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs)
based on the Ribosomal Database Project (RDP) by UPARSE with a 97 %
similarity cutoff after the raw reads were quality filtered and merged by
fastx, Cutadapt, Usearch and FLASH.Mothur was used to perform rare -
faction analysis and calculate the community richness index and alpha
diversities, including the Shannon and Simpson indexes. Sample tree
cluster by Bray-Curtis distance matrix and an unweighted pair-group
method with arithmetic means (UPGMA) and Jaccard principal coor -
dinate analysis (PCoA) based on OTUs were performed using R Project
(Vegan package, V3.3.1). Redundancy analysis (RDA) was analysed by
Canoco for Windows 4.5 (Microcomputer Power, NY, USA), which was
assessed by MCPP with 499 random permutations.
2.5. Quantitative analysis of BA in mice serum
Mice serum that were stored at 80
◦
C were thawed in an ice bath to
reduce sample degradation, and samples were prepared according to
previously published methods [ 19 , 20 ]. A quantitativefull spectrum
analysis of bile acids was performed by Metabo-Pro fi le Biotechnology
(Shanghai) Co., Ltd (UPLC-MS/MS, ACQUITY UPLC-Xevo TQ-S, Waters
Corp., Milford, MA, USA).

Total RNA was extracted from frozen liver tissue using an RNA
extraction kit (TaKaRa, Japan; cat. no. 9767) according to the manu -
facturer ’ s instructions. FXR and TRG5 primers were designed by Sangon
Biotech (Shanghai, China). The primer sequences of FXR were as fol -

Transcription was carried out using the PrimeScript ™ RT Master Mix Kit

2.7. Western blotting analysis
The expression of FXR and TGR5 protein in the liver tissue were
detected by western blotting. Sample preparation and extraction was
performed according to standard protocols [ 26 ]. Proteins were sepa -
rated using 10 % SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes
(Bio-Rad,USA), where they were blocked with 5% nonfat milk in
TBS-Tween 20 (TBST) for 1 h. The membranes were then incubated with
primary antibodies at 4 ℃ overnight. The primary antibodies FXR
monoclonal antibody, 1:500 dilution, Cell Signaling, Cat. no. 72105S;
TGR5 monoclonal antibody, 1:1000, Abcam, Cat. no. ab72608; β -Actin
monoclonal antibody, 1:5000 dilution, Multi Science Biotech, Cat. no.
ab008.The secondary antibodies horseradish peroxidase
[HRP]-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG, 1:5000 dilution, Multi Science
Biotech, Cat. no. GAM0072 ; HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG,
1:5000 dilution, Multi Science Biotech, Cat. no. GAR0072 were incu -
bated at room temperature for 1 h. Blot were developed with enhanced
chemiluminescence (ECL) and signals captured with the Odyssey Fc
(LI-COR), USA.
2.8. Statistical analysis
The SPSS 22.0 software was used for Statistical analysis. Data are
presented as the means ± standard deviation. The significant differences
between and within the different groups were examined using one-way
ANOVAs, followed by Duncan ’ s multiple-range test. P < 0.05 was
considered statistically significant.

3.3. Modification in the composition of gut microbiota after PTFC
treatment
16S rDNA sequencing analysis was used to investigate the structural
changes in the gut microbiota in mice that received PTFC treatment. In
total, 644541 useable reads were obtained from 15 samples, and 678
OTUs were collected at a 97 % similarity level. In this work, Mice that
fed with HFD, showed decreased microbial diversity and richness
demonstrated by both the Community richness index and Shannon
index. Significant decreases in Chao1 and ACE, indicating lower
microbiota community diversity, were found in the High and PTFC
groups ( P < 0.01, Fig. 3 A – C). The Rank-abundance curve, Sample
Rarefaction curve,Sample Shannon curves and Species accumulation
curves show that most of the diversity and new phylotypes were covered
and the amount of sequencing data is reasonable ( Fig. 3 D – G).
3.4. Beta-diversity analyses between three groups
Beta-diversity analyses including principal component Analysis
(PCA) and hierarchical cluster analysis, were carried out to further
provide an overview of the effects of HFD and PTFC treatments on the
composition and structure of gut microbiota. PCA revealed a clear sep -
aration between the Normal and High groups ( Fig. 4 A,B). As expected,
the composition of gut microbiota exhibited a obvious response to PTFC
intervention. According to Lefse analyses, different colours represent
different groups. The annotation of the phylum level is displayed on the
outermost ring, while the annotation information of the other levels is
displayed in Fig. 4 C,D. Bacteroidaceae and Rikenellaceaewere increased
in the PTFC group at the family level ( P < 0.05). Porphyromonadaceae
and Enterococcaceaewere increased in the HFD group at the family level
( P < 0.05).
3.5. Venn diagram analasis between three groups
From the Venn diagram, the unique OTUs and the common OTUs of
each group indicated the unique species information of each group more
directly. Different numbers of OTUs were detected in each group, i.e.,
638 in the normal group, 478 in the HFD group, and 458 in the PTFC
group ( Fig. 5 ). Among all OTUs, 385 were shared by all groups. Addi -
tionally, each group had unique OTUs, including 132 in the normal
group,4 in the HFD group, and 21 in the PTFC group.

3.7. PICRUSt analysis and prediction of genomic functional changes
among three groups
Based on the 16S rDNA and reference sequence database, PICRUSt
predicted the macrogenome functional composition of the flora. The
accuracy of the method was 84 – 95 %. In the PTFC group, 12 KEGG
pathways were altered, including energy metabolism, amino acid
metabolism, ethylbenzene degradation and peptidoglycan biosynthesis
( Fig. 7 I). Compared with the HFD group, other ion-coupled transporters
were upregulatedand beta-alanine metabolism, type I diabetes mellitus,
ethylene degradation, energy metabolism, alanine, aspartate and
glutamate metabolism were reduced ( Fig. 7 J). These significant
pathway changes predicted that PTFC treatment could improve the gut
microbiota structure of mice under the condition of HFD feeding, thus
exerting a therapeutic effect against NASH in mice.
3.8. The effect of PTFC on serum bile acid dysregulation of NASH mice
A reciprocal stepwise decrease in secondary BAs (mean: 62.57 %,
44.12 %, and 49.64 % in Normal control, HFD, and PTFC, respectively)
across the three groups ( P = 0.01) ( Fig. 8 B), PTFC increased the ratio of
secondary to primary bile acids. Campared with the Normal group, Total
Bile Acids in HFD group increased ( Fig. 8 C, P < 0.05). Compared with
the Normal group, the serum bile acid from the HFD group showed
significantly increased levels of TDCA, DCA, TCA, CA, and significantly
decreased levels of muroCA, TUDCA. PTFC reduced the content of toxic
bile acids, such as TDCA, DCA, TCA, CA ( Fig. 9 , P < 0.05).
3.9. PTFC can increase the FXR and TGR5 protein level and mRNA
expression
Compared with mice in the Normal group, those in the HFD group
showed a signi fi cant decrease in the FXR and TGR5 protein level and
mRNA expression in the liver tissue ( Fig. 10 A1, A2, B1, B2, P < 0.01;
P < 0.05). Compared with the HFD group, the PTFC exhibited a
significantly higher FXR protein level expression in the liver tissue, and
also showed significantly higher TGR5 protein level and mRNA
expression in liver tissue ( Fig. 10 A1,B1, P < 0.01; P < 0.05). There
were no signi fi cant di ff ;erences in the FXR mRNA expression between
mice in the HFD and PTFC groups ( Fig. 10 A2, P > 0.05).
4. Discussion
NASH has become a major cause of cirrhosis and has been recognized
as a major HCC catalyst, which is often associated with obesity, dysli -
pidemia and insulin resistance. So far, the underlying mechanism of the

11
occurrence and progression of NASH has not been fully elucidated. The
lack of effective treatment has drawn great attention. In recent years,
more and more evidences indicate that the “ gut – liver ” axis is implicated
in the occurrence and progression of NASH. And the modification of
“ gut-liver ” axis has been considered as a potential treatment for the
management of NASH [ 7 ]. The gut microbiota, foundational element of
the “ gut-liver ” axis, are well known to be significantly altered in NASH
animal models and patients with NASH [ 8 ]. Bile acid is typically asso -
ciated with the gut microbiota and are synthesized in the liver from
cholesterol and metabolized in the gut. The gut microbiota regulates bile
acid production and signalling via the biotransformation of intestinal
bile acids to unconjugated and secondary forms that readily activate bile
acid receptors. Bile acids are ligands for FXR and TGR5. The profiles of
bile acids and gut microbiota influence each other; bile acids can
modulate microbiota composition, which in turn regulates the size and
composition of the bile acid pool.
In our previous studies, we found that PTFC treatment could alleviate
NAFLD by regulating the TLR/CCL inflammatory signaling pathways,
the SIRT1/PGC-1 α pathways and Th17/treg balance [ 16 – 22 ]. However,
the specific mechanism requires further study. In this study, we aimed to
determine the preventive effects of PTFC on high-fat-diet (HFD)-induced
NAFLD in mice and the underlying mechanism focusing on gut micro -
biota and bile acid metabolism.
In our study, we found that compared with the Normal group, HFD-
induced NAFLD mice had differences at the phylum, class, and genus
levels that resulted in gut microbiota dysbiosis. These changes were

dramatic decrease in the Christensenellaceae family compared to that in

To study the underlying mechanism of PTFC in treating NASH, we
investigated the positive effect of PTFC on the intestinal microbiota. In
this study, at the family level, compared with the Normal group, the
relative abundance of Christensenellaceae and Erysipelotrichaceaewas
decreased in the HFD group. After PTFC treatment, the relative abun -
dance of Christensenellaceae and Erysipelotrichaceae were significantly
increased. The relative abundance of Porphyromonadaceae and Strep -
tococcaceaeincreased in the HFD group. After PTFC treatment, the
relative abundance of Porphyromonadaceae and Streptococcaceae was
significantly decreased. Christensenellaceae, a recently described family
in the phylum Firmicutes, is emerging as an important player in human
health [ 23 ]. Christensenellaceae is reported to bereduced in individuals
with metabolic syndrome (MetS) compared to the level in healthy
controls [ 24 ]. Stachyose improved the intestinal homeostasis of HFD-fed
mice by improving the bacterial diversity with increases in the relative
abundance of Christensenellaceae [ 25 ]. Erysipelotrichaceae was nega -
tively correlated with body weight,while Porphyromonadaceae was
positively correlated with body weight [ 26 ]. At the family level, Strep -
tococcaceae was enriched in the NAFLD group [ 27 , 28 ].

At the genus level, after treatment with PTFC, the abundance of the
beneficial bacteria with protective effects in the body increased. The
abundance of Bacteroides in the PTFC group increased, and Akker -
mansiaincreased at a ratio of 4.4 %. Akkermansia has been inversely
associated with obesity, diabetes, inflammation, and metabolic disor -
ders [ 29 , 30 ]. Due to its highly promising probiotic activities against
obesity and diabetes, Akkermansia has drawn intense interest in the
context ofresearch and development in recent years [ 31 ].
The KEGG database was used to identify the relationship between
metabolic function and host metabolites. In the PTFC group, 12 KEGG
pathways were altered, including energy metabolism, amino acid
metabolism, ethylene degradation and peptidoglycan biosynthesis.
Among them, bile acid is the key factor in regulating energy metabolism
[ 32 ]. Compared with the HFD group, other ion-coupled transporters
were upregulated, and beta-alanine metabolism, type I diabetes melli -
tus, ethylene degradation, energy metabolism, and alanine, aspartate
and glutamate metabolisms were reduced. These significant pathway
changes predicted that PTFC treatment could improve the gut micro -
biota structure of mice under the condition of HFD, thus exerting a
therapeutic effect on NAFLD in mice.
Studies have shown that NASH patients present dysbiosis associated
with increases in BA synthesis, fecal primary BA and the primary:sec -
ondary BA ratio [ 33 ]. FXR is an important therapeutic target for NAFLD.
The FXR agonist obeticholic acid significantly improve the pathological
characteristics of patients with NASH, indicating its potential value in
the treatment of NASH [ 34 ]. DCA is also a natural FXR antagonist, CDCA
is an important natural FXR agonist [ 35 ]. TGR5 agonist is a potentially
therapeutic action against metabolic diseases such as NAFLD/NASH
[ 36 ]. TGR5 was activated by bile acids in the order DCA > CDCA > CA
[ 37 ]. Our results indicate that TDCA, TCA and DCA levels in the serum of
mice with NASH significantly increased, while the level of HDCA,
muroCA significantly decreased. PTFC treatment, however, significantly
reduced the levels of TDCA, DCA, TCA, and CA in the serum. Our results
also showed that mice with NASH have FXR and TGR5 deficiency and
that PTFC can help activate FXR and TGR5, potentially through the
regulation of bile acid metabolism.
In summary, we have demonstrated significant changes in compo -
sition of bile acids and gut microbiota dysbiosis in NASH mice induced
by HFD. Our study showed that PTFC intervention significantly
increased the relative abundances of Bacteroidaceae and Christense -
nellaceae. Furthermore, PTFC reduced the content of toxic bile acids,
such as TDCA, DCA, TCA, CA and increased the ratio of secondary to
primary bile acids. FXR and TGR5 deficiency were significantly allevi -
ated. PTFC can regulate “ gut-liver ” axis to play an important therapeutic
role in NASH.
5. Conclusions
In this study, we revealed that PTFC has a significant regulatory ef -
fect on gut microbiota dysbiosis and bile acid metabolism in NASH mice.
The results showed that PTFC increased the richness of the intestinal
flora, adjusted the structure of the gut microbial community, and
increased the relative abundances of the Bacteroideae, Christense -
nellaceae and Akkermansia. In addition, after treatment with PTFC in
NASH mice, TDCA, DCA, TCA, CA were significantly decreased, FXR and
TGR5 expression were increased. Therefore, our results indicate that the
gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism play an important role in the
progression of NASH, and PTFC attenuate NASH via regulating the gut
microbiota and bile acid metabolism in mice.
